title: Explicit QEMU Standard VGA PCI identity 1234:1111
evidence:
Name                   : Microsoft Basic Display Adapter
PNPDeviceID            : PCI\VEN_1234&DEV_1111&SUBSYS_00000000&REV_02\3&11583659&1&08
Manufacturer           : (Standard display types)
Service                : BasicDisplay
Status                 : OK
ConfigManagerErrorCode : 0
[raw/pnp.txt; exact inner query raw/pnp.command.txt]

bare_metal.expectation: A physical GPU normally exposes its hardware vendor/device pair. QEMU documents 1234:1111 as Standard VGA. The generic Microsoft display driver alone is not evidence. A spoofed FPGA/device could implement this identity, so the ID establishes the exposed virtual-device identity, not a mathematical proof against arbitrary adversarial hardware.

repro: From the output directory run: Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity | Where-Object PNPDeviceID -like 'PCI\VEN_1234&DEV_1111*' | Format-List Name,PNPDeviceID,Service. The original broad command is saved in raw/pnp.command.txt.

bare_metal.expectation: A genuine controller should expose the controller vendor IEEE/RAC OUI and internally consistent capacity. Raw IEEE bytes 00 54 52 exactly match QEMU default initialization (read as OUI 52:54:00). OACS=0x012B advertises Namespace Management/Attachment (bit 3), making TNVMCAP supported; it is zero despite the active 274877906944-byte namespace. A 2TB drive can legitimately have a smaller namespace, so the 256GiB/model-name mismatch alone is a clue. These protocol fields jointly fingerprint QEMU and contradict a conforming controller; defective or spoofed physical firmware remains an alternative.

repro: From the output directory run & .\probes\DeviceProbe.exe nvme raw\nvme-repeat. It opens PhysicalDrive0 for read and issues only IOCTL_STORAGE_QUERY_PROPERTY, Identify Controller and Namespace. Source and build: probes/DeviceProbe.cs and raw/deviceprobe-build.txt. Compile: & 'C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\csc.exe' /nologo /platform:x64 /optimize+ /out:probes\DeviceProbe.exe probes\DeviceProbe.cs. Parse bytes 73-75 (IEEE), 256-257 (OACS), 280-295 (TNVMCAP) of the 4096-byte controller payload. Namespace NSZE and NCAP are at 0 and 8; LBAF[FLBAS & 15].LBADS=9.

title: ACPI FWCF device preserves the QEMU fw_cfg register layout with a generic HID
evidence:
DSDT length=10070 checksumSum=0
AML Device FWCF nameOffset=0x2334 expectedPackageMatch=True
Verbatim device bytes: 5B-82-29-46-57-43-46-08-5F-48-49-44-0C-41-D0-0C-02-08-5F-53-54-41-0A-0B-08-5F-43-52-53-11-0D-0A-0A-47-01-10-05-10-05-01-0C-79-00
Decoded restricted AML: Device (FWCF); Name (_HID, EisaId (PNP0C02)); Name (_STA, 0x0B); Name (_CRS, ResourceTemplate { IO (Decode16, 0x0510, 0x0510, 0x01, 0x0C) })
Interpretation: device reserves I/O 0x510-0x51B, matching the QEMU fw_cfg selector/data and DMA register block. No I/O access or ACPI method evaluation was performed.

bare_metal.expectation: Ordinary physical MSI/AMI firmware has no need for the QEMU fw_cfg virtual firmware interface. The AML name FWCF, status 0x0B and exact 12-byte I/O resource at 0x510 match QEMU fw_cfg source. This guest uses generic EISA HID PNP0C02 where upstream uses QEMU0002. Generic PNP0C02 alone is common on physical PCs; the finding is the combined named-device/resource implementation match. Direct I/O signature QEMU or DMA signature QEMU CFG was not read: that would require kernel I/O privileges/driver. Thus this is a strong implementation fingerprint rather than a live protocol-signature proof.

repro: Run powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\collect-firmware.ps1 to save current registry ACPI tables, then powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\probes\InspectFwcfgAml.ps1. It validates exact AML bytes and checksum rather than evaluating any AML. Registry source: HKLM:\HARDWARE\ACPI\DSDT\ALASKA\A_M_I\00000001 value 00000000. Current name offset 0x2334. The restricted decoder is specific to the observed AML package and deliberately fails if its encoding changes.
